name: Egusi Soup
description: A thick, hearty soup made from ground melon seeds, leafy greens, and assorted proteins. One of Nigeria's most beloved soups.

recipe.tips: Fry the egusi in palm oil before adding stock — this gives it a richer, nuttier flavor and prevents a watery texture.
variations: Use uziza leaves instead of bitterleaf
Add okra for a draw version
Use oha leaves for the Igbo variant

steps.instruction: Season beef and ponmo with onion, crayfish, and seasoning cubes. Cook until tender and reserve the stock.
Heat palm oil in a pot over medium heat. Fry blended tomatoes and scotch bonnet until the oil rises — about 15 minutes.
Add ground egusi to the pot and fry, stirring constantly, for 8–10 minutes until it clumps and turns golden.
Pour in the meat stock, add iru, crayfish, and seasoning. Simmer for 10 minutes.
Add cooked meat, stockfish, and smoked fish. Stir and cook for 5 minutes.
Add washed bitterleaf, stir, and cook for 5 minutes. Do not overcook the leaves.
Taste, adjust seasoning, and serve with pounded yam or eba.

name: Jollof Rice
description: Nigeria's most iconic rice dish — cooked in a rich tomato-pepper sauce. The centerpiece of every party and the subject of West Africa's greatest culinary debate.

recipe.tips: The secret to smoky party Jollof is high heat at the end with the lid on. Use parboiled long-grain rice. Never lift the lid during cooking.
variations: Use chicken stock instead of water for extra depth
Add bay leaves and thyme
Finish with a knob of butter

ingredients.name: Red Bell Pepper (Tatashe)
substitutes: roasted red peppers in a jar

steps.instruction: Blend tomatoes, tatashe, scotch bonnet, and half an onion into a smooth purée.
Heat oil in a pot. Fry diced onion for 2 minutes, then add tomato paste and fry for 3 minutes.
Add the blended pepper mixture. Cook, stirring occasionally, until the oil floats on top — about 20–25 minutes.
Add chicken stock, seasoning cubes, curry, thyme, and bay leaves. Stir well.
Parboil the rice for 8 minutes, drain, and add to the pot. Liquid should barely cover the rice.
Cover tightly and cook on medium-low for 20 minutes. Do not stir or uncover.
Uncover, fold from bottom to top, re-cover, and cook on low for 10 more minutes.
For the smoky finish, cook on high for 3–5 minutes until you hear crackling at the bottom. Rest before serving.

name: Pounded Yam
description: Smooth, stretchy, and deeply satisfying — pounded yam is Nigeria's most prized swallow. Made by boiling and pounding white yam into a silky dough.

recipe.tips: Pound while the yam is still very hot — cold yam will not smooth out. Add hot water sparingly, one tablespoon at a time.
variations: Mix with cocoyam for Igbo-style pounded yam
Use instant pounded yam powder for a quick version

steps.instruction: Peel, wash, and cut yam into even chunks.
Boil in salted water until very soft and fork-tender, about 25–30 minutes.
Drain completely — no water should remain in the pot.
Transfer hot yam to a mortar and pound, folding and turning between strokes.
Add hot water one tablespoon at a time if needed to keep it smooth.
Pound until completely smooth, elastic, and lump-free — about 10–15 minutes.
Shape into balls with wet hands and serve immediately with your soup of choice.

name: Suya
description: Nigeria's most iconic street food — thin strips of beef coated in yaji spice and grilled over open flame. Sold at roadside spots across the country every evening.

recipe.tips: Slice beef very thin — 5mm against the grain. Thin slices absorb spice better and cook fast. Marinate overnight for the best flavor.
variations: Use chicken thighs instead of beef
Try ram meat for Sallah-style suya

ingredients.name: Yaji (Suya Spice)
ingredients.notes: ground kuli-kuli, ginger, paprika, pepper, garlic, onion powder, salt

steps.instruction: Mix yaji spice with groundnut oil to form a paste.
Coat each beef strip thoroughly in the spice paste.
Thread strips onto flat skewers, 2–3 pieces per skewer.
Marinate in the fridge for at least 1 hour — overnight is better.
Grill over charcoal or on a hot grill pan, turning every 3–4 minutes until cooked and lightly charred.
Dust with extra yaji and serve with sliced onions and tomatoes.

name: Moi Moi
description: Savory steamed bean pudding made from blended black-eyed peas and peppers. A fixture at parties and family meals — often filled with fish, egg, or liver.

recipe.tips: Blend the beans very smoothly — lumpy batter won't set properly. Season the raw batter well before steaming.
variations: Fill with hard-boiled eggs
Use plantain leaves for an authentic smoky flavor
Add corned beef or sardines as filling

steps.instruction: Soak beans overnight. Rub between palms and rinse until all skins are removed.
Blend peeled beans with peppers and onion into a very smooth batter.
Add crayfish, seasoning, oil, and salt. Mix well. The batter should be well-seasoned.
Grease your containers. Pour batter ¾ full, add filling in the center.
Place containers in a pot with 2–3 inches of boiling water. Steam for 40–45 minutes.
Check with a knife — it should come out clean. Cool slightly before unmolding.

name: Akara
description: Deep-fried bean fritters — crispy on the outside, fluffy inside. A quintessential Nigerian breakfast, usually sold by roadside vendors in the morning.

recipe.tips: After blending, whisk the batter vigorously for 2 minutes to incorporate air — this is what makes akara fluffy, not dense. Oil must be very hot before adding batter.
variations: Add diced onion and crayfish to the batter
Stuff with spiced filling before frying

steps.instruction: Blend peeled beans with scotch bonnet and onion using a little water until very smooth.
Pour into a bowl. Whisk vigorously for 2 minutes to incorporate air.
Add crayfish, seasoning, and salt. Mix well.
Heat oil to 180°C (350°F) — at least 2 inches deep.
Drop tablespoonfuls of batter into the oil. Do not overcrowd.
Fry until golden on both sides, about 3–4 minutes. Drain on paper towels and serve hot.

name: Efo Riro
description: A vibrant Yoruba vegetable soup made with leafy greens, assorted meats, iru, and crayfish in a rich pepper base. Simple to make, deeply flavorful.

recipe.tips: Add the greens last and cook for no more than 5 minutes to preserve color and nutrients. Iru is essential — don't skip it.
variations: Use spinach or ugu interchangeably
Add stockfish for extra depth
Make vegetarian with tofu

steps.instruction: Cook seasoned beef and ponmo until tender. Reserve the stock.
Heat palm oil. Fry sliced onion for 2 minutes, then add iru and fry until fragrant.
Add coarsely blended peppers and cook until oil rises — about 20 minutes.
Add meat, stock, smoked fish, crayfish, and seasoning. Simmer for 5 minutes.
Add chopped greens, stir, cover and cook for 3–5 minutes. Do not overcook.
Serve with pounded yam or eba.

name: Pepper Soup
description: A light but intensely spiced broth made with assorted meat or fish and native pepper soup spices. Served as a starter, at naming ceremonies, or as a cold remedy.

recipe.tips: Don't cover the pot completely — it should reduce and concentrate. The broth should be clear, not thick. Season aggressively.
variations: Use catfish for point-and-kill pepper soup
Add cocoyam chunks to make it more filling
Goat head pepper soup for festive occasions

steps.instruction: Place meat in a pot with onion, garlic, ginger, salt, and seasoning. Cook dry on medium for 5 minutes to render juices.
Add water to cover. Bring to a boil and skim off foam.
Add pepper soup spice mix, crayfish, and scotch bonnet. Cook for 30–40 minutes until meat is tender.
Add uziza leaves. Cook for 5 more minutes.
Taste and adjust — the broth should be intensely flavored. Serve hot.

name: Fried Plantain (Dodo)
description: Ripe plantains fried until golden and caramelized. A universal side dish to almost every Nigerian meal — also eaten as a snack on its own.

recipe.tips: Use fully ripe plantains — skin should be mostly black. Medium heat is key: too hot burns the outside before the inside cooks.
variations: Season with chili powder and salt before frying
Bake at 200°C for a healthier version

steps.instruction: Peel plantains and slice diagonally, about 1cm thick.
Heat oil in a pan over medium heat — enough to come halfway up the slices.
Fry in a single layer for 3–4 minutes per side until deep golden and caramelized.
Drain on paper towels, sprinkle with salt, and serve immediately.

name: Banga Soup (Ofe Akwu)
description: A rich, aromatic soup made from palm fruit extract. The Igbo and Urhobo versions differ in spice profile. One of the most soul-satisfying soups in Nigerian cuisine.

recipe.tips: Extracting the palm fruit properly is key — boil, pound, and squeeze out all the juice. The soup's richness comes entirely from the palm fruit concentrate.
variations: Urhobo version uses banga spices (oburunbebe stick, dried atama leaves)
Igbo version uses uziza and utazi leaves
Use canned palm fruit concentrate to save time

ingredients.name: Palm Fruit (Fresh or Canned)
ingredients.notes: fresh, or 1 can palm fruit concentrate

steps.instruction: If using fresh palm fruit: boil for 30 minutes, pound in a mortar, add warm water, and squeeze out the juice through a sieve. Discard the pulp.
Pour the palm fruit juice into a pot and bring to a boil. Allow to cook and thicken for 15 minutes.
Add cooked meat, stockfish, smoked fish, and onion. Stir.
Add crayfish, scotch bonnet, banga spice (if using), and seasoning. Simmer for 15 minutes.
Add uziza or atama leaves. Cook for 5 more minutes. Serve with pounded yam or starch.

name: Okra Soup
description: A viscous, protein-rich soup made with fresh or dried okra. Quick to prepare and eaten across all regions — sometimes combined with egusi for extra body.

recipe.tips: Don't overcook the okra — 5–7 minutes max to keep the draw texture. Slice, don't blend, for the best results.
variations: Add egusi for a combined okra-egusi soup
Use frozen okra when fresh is unavailable
Add ogiri for a deeper, earthier flavor

steps.instruction: Cook seasoned beef and stockfish until tender. Reserve stock.
Heat palm oil in a pot. Add blended pepper and iru. Fry for 5 minutes.
Add meat stock, crayfish, and seasoning. Simmer for 5 minutes.
Add meat, stockfish, and smoked fish. Cook for 3 minutes.
Add sliced okra. Stir and cook for 5–7 minutes — no more. Serve with eba or pounded yam.

name: Coconut Rice
description: Fragrant rice cooked in coconut milk — a beloved coastal Nigerian dish, usually paired with fried chicken and dodo.

recipe.tips: Use full-fat coconut milk. Toast the rice in the pot for 2 minutes before adding liquid for extra flavor.
variations: Add shrimp and peppers for a one-pot meal
Use fresh coconut cream for more intensity

steps.instruction: Heat oil, sauté diced onion for 2 minutes.
Add washed rice and toast for 2 minutes, stirring.
Pour in coconut milk and stock. Add seasoning, curry, and thyme. Stir once.
Bring to a boil, reduce to lowest heat, cover tightly, and cook for 20–25 minutes. Do not uncover.
Fluff with a fork and serve with fried chicken and dodo.

name: Ogbono Soup
description: A thick draw soup made from ground wild mango seeds. Known for its distinctive stretchy texture and deep nutty flavor — often combined with okra or egusi.

recipe.tips: Fry the ogbono in palm oil before adding liquid — this activates its draw and deepens the flavor. Don't stir too aggressively once the draw develops.
variations: Combine with okra for extra draw
Add leafy greens at the end
Add egusi for a richer version

steps.instruction: Cook seasoned beef and stockfish until tender. Reserve stock.
Heat palm oil over medium heat. Add ground ogbono and fry, stirring, for 3–5 minutes until it dissolves and becomes fragrant.
Gradually add meat stock, stirring as you pour. The soup will become thick and draw immediately.
Add iru, crayfish, pepper, and seasoning. Simmer for 10 minutes.
Add cooked meat, stockfish, and smoked fish. Cook for 5 minutes.
Add greens if using. Cook for 3 minutes and serve with eba or pounded yam.

name: Nkwobi
description: A spicy Igbo delicacy made from cow foot cooked in a palm oil and utazi leaf sauce. A popular bar snack and party delicacy in the South East.

recipe.tips: Cook the cow foot until very tender — it should be gelatinous, not chewy. The utazi leaf gives the characteristic bitter note; don't skip it.
variations: Use goat head instead of cow foot
Add snail for Isiewu-style

steps.instruction: Season cow foot with onion, seasoning, and salt. Pressure cook for 45–60 minutes until very tender.
In a bowl, mix palm oil with dissolved potash water. Stir vigorously — it will turn yellow and thicken.
Add blended pepper, crayfish, and seasoning to the palm oil mixture. Mix well.
Add the cooked cow foot and toss until every piece is coated.
Top generously with sliced utazi leaves and additional onion rings. Serve warm.

name: Ofada Rice and Ayamase
description: Locally grown unpolished Nigerian rice served with Ayamase — a fiery green pepper stew made with assorted offal and bleached palm oil. A Yoruba classic.

recipe.tips: The bleached palm oil (cooked until it clears from orange to yellow) is what gives Ayamase its unique flavor and dark color. Don't rush this step.
variations: Use regular rice if Ofada is unavailable
Serve with fried plantain and boiled eggs

steps.instruction: Cook Ofada rice separately. It takes longer than regular rice — wash well and boil until tender, about 40 minutes.
Bleach palm oil: heat in an open pot on high until it turns light yellow and smoke appears — about 10 minutes. Let cool.
Blend green peppers and scotch bonnet coarsely. Set aside.
Cook seasoned assorted offal until tender. Reserve stock.
Heat bleached palm oil. Add iru and sliced onion, fry for 2 minutes.
Add blended green pepper. Fry until dry and the oil rises — about 20 minutes.
Add cooked offal, stock, crayfish, and seasoning. Simmer for 10 minutes.
Serve Ofada rice wrapped in uma leaves (or on a plate) with Ayamase stew and boiled eggs.

name: Groundnut Soup
description: A rich, nutty soup made from ground roasted peanuts — popular in the North and among the Tiv people. Deep, satisfying, and pairs well with tuwo or pounded yam.

recipe.tips: Roast the peanuts yourself and grind them — pre-ground peanut butter gives a different texture. Add the groundnut paste in batches to avoid lumps.
variations: Add sweet potato for a thicker, sweeter version
Use chicken instead of beef

steps.instruction: Cook seasoned beef until tender. Reserve stock.
In the same pot, fry blended tomatoes, pepper, and onion until oil rises — about 15 minutes.
Mix ground peanuts with a little warm water to loosen into a paste.
Add peanut paste to the pot in batches, stirring after each addition.
Add meat stock, crayfish, and seasoning. Stir and simmer for 20 minutes until oil floats on top.
Add cooked beef. Cook for 5 more minutes. Serve with tuwo shinkafa or pounded yam.

name: Eba (Garri)
description: A starchy swallow made by dissolving garri (cassava flakes) in boiling water. One of Nigeria's most affordable and widespread staple foods — eaten by millions daily.

recipe.tips: Use boiling water — not warm. Add garri gradually while stirring to avoid lumps. Cover and let steam for 2 minutes before molding for a smoother texture.
variations: Use yellow garri for a slightly sour flavor
Add a little butter for a richer taste

steps.instruction: Bring water to a rolling boil in a pot.
Gradually pour garri into the water while stirring constantly with a wooden spoon.
Stir and fold until it forms a smooth, firm dough with no lumps.
Cover and steam on low heat for 2 minutes.
Scoop into balls with a wet spoon and serve with any Nigerian soup.

name: Tuwo Shinkafa
description: A smooth, thick swallow made from soft rice. The Northern Nigerian staple — typically served with miyan kuka (baobab leaf soup) or miyan taushe (pumpkin soup).

recipe.tips: Use a starchy short-grain or soft rice — not basmati. Overcook the rice intentionally. The more you stir and mash, the smoother the tuwo.
variations: Add a little more water for a softer consistency

steps.instruction: Wash rice and cook with water until very soft and overcooked — about 30 minutes.
Reduce heat to the lowest setting. Stir and mash continuously with a wooden spoon.
Keep mashing and folding until the rice is fully smooth with no visible grains.
It should pull away from the sides of the pot when ready.
Mold into balls with a wet spoon. Serve with miyan kuka or miyan taushe.

name: Ofe Onugbu (Bitter Leaf Soup)
description: A bold, slightly bitter Igbo soup made with bitter leaves, cocoyam paste, and assorted meats. A staple of Igbo traditional cuisine — rich, hearty, and deeply satisfying.

recipe.tips: Wash and squeeze the bitter leaves thoroughly to remove excess bitterness — taste as you go. The cocoyam paste is what thickens this soup, not flour.
variations: Add oha leaves for a mixed version
Use spinach if bitter leaves are unavailable (very different flavor)

steps.instruction: Boil cocoyam until very soft. Pound in a mortar until smooth. Set aside.
Cook seasoned beef and stockfish in a pot with onion and seasoning until tender. Reserve stock.
Add palm oil to the stock pot. Bring to a boil.
Drop cocoyam paste in small balls into the boiling soup to thicken. Stir gently until dissolved.
Add ogiri, crayfish, blended pepper, and seasoning. Stir and simmer for 10 minutes.
Add meat, stockfish, and smoked fish. Cook for 5 minutes.
Add washed bitterleaf. Stir and cook for 5–7 minutes. Serve with pounded yam.

name: Afang Soup
description: A prized Cross River and Akwa Ibom soup made with afang leaves and waterleaf, combined with seafood and assorted meats. Known for its unique green color and rich flavor.

recipe.tips: Afang leaves should be blended or ground very finely — they're tough and fibrous. Waterleaf releases a lot of water when cooked, so add it before afang and let it reduce first.
variations: Add periwinkle for extra richness
Use snail as additional protein

steps.instruction: Cook seasoned beef and stockfish until tender. Reserve stock.
Add palm oil to the stock pot. Add crayfish, pepper, and seasoning. Simmer for 5 minutes.
Add waterleaf. Stir and cook for 5 minutes until it wilts and releases its water.
Add periwinkle if using. Stir.
Add ground afang leaves. Stir well and cook for 5–7 minutes. Do not overcook — it should stay vibrant.
Taste, adjust seasoning, and serve with pounded yam or eba.
